exercises.prompt: Implement sign(n) so it returns 1 when n is positive, -1 when n is negative, and 0 when n is exactly zero.
hints: Three outcomes means three branches: positive, negative, and exactly zero — handle them with if statements.
Compare against zero: n > 0 is the positive case and n < 0 is the negative one; whatever is left must be zero.
Write if (n > 0) return 1, then if (n < 0) return -1, and a final return 0 for the rest.

exercises.prompt: Implement letterGrade(score) so it returns the letter grade for a 0-100 score: 'A' for 90 and above, 'B' for 80 to 89, 'C' for 70 to 79, 'D' for 60 to 69, and 'F' for anything below 60.
exercises.solution:
function letterGrade(score) {
  if (score >= 90) return 'A'
  if (score >= 80) return 'B'
  if (score >= 70) return 'C'
  if (score >= 60) return 'D'
  return 'F'
}
hints: Check the grades from the highest threshold down, so each later test only has to handle the scores that did not already match.
Once 90-and-up has returned 'A', a plain score >= 80 is enough to mean 'B'.
Chain if (score >= 90) return 'A', then >= 80, >= 70, >= 60, and a final return 'F'.

exercises.prompt: Implement isLeapYear(year) so it returns true when year is a leap year. A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, except that years divisible by 100 are not — unless they are also divisible by 400. So 2000 and 2024 are leap years, while 1900 and 2023 are not.
hints: This is a single boolean expression: combine the divisible-by-4 rule with the century exception using && and ||.
Divisibility is a remainder test — year % 4 === 0 — and the exception is 'not divisible by 100, or divisible by 400', which is an || of two tests.
return year % 4 === 0 && (year % 100 !== 0 || year % 400 === 0); keep the parentheses so the || groups first.

exercises.prompt: Implement clamp(value, low, high) so it constrains value to the range low..high: return low when value is below low, high when value is above high, and value itself when it already sits within the range. Assume low <= high.
hints: There are three possibilities — value is below the range, above it, or already inside — and each returns a different thing.
A ternary can chain: value < low ? low : (decide between high and value for the rest).
return value < low ? low : value > high ? high : value covers below, above, and within in one line.

exercises.prompt: Implement exactlyOne(a, b), where a and b are booleans, so it returns true when exactly one of them is true — that is, when they differ. When both are true or both are false, return false.
hints: Exactly one true means at least one is true, but not both — two conditions joined together.
At least one is a || b; both is a && b; flip a boolean with the ! operator.
return (a || b) && !(a && b) — either one holds, minus the case where both do.
